newsitem.title: SPAIN: INTERVIEW-Soros warns British pound is overvalued.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Soros warns British pound is overvalued.

text.p: International financier George Soros, the man credited with almost single-handedly driving the British pound out of the Exchange Rate Mechanism in 1992, warned on Wednesday that sterling was overvalued against the mark.

In an interview with Reuters, the global fund manager said while he believed the pound was unlikely to join Europe's economic and monetary union at the start in 1999, he was sure Spain, Italy and Portugal would.
He also said he had become more optimistic that the single currency would be launched on time.

On sterling, Soros, whose flagship investment fund Quantum is credited with making some $1 billion from sterling's exit from the ERM, said he believed the currency had appreciated too much against the mark.
"I think the pound is overvalued, too strong, against the mark and European currencies," Soros told Reuters after awarding a cultural prize in Madrid.
"However, I don't think the rate against the dollar is worrisome at all," he added.

UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown said earlier on Wednesday that he shared industry and exporters concerns about sterling's relentless rise. A survey showed that the currency's strength was denting exporters confidence as their products become more expensive on world markets.

Sterling has appreciated more than 19 percent since last August to five-year peaks at above 2.93 marks in late Europe trade on Wednesday. Traders are predicting that the currency will now likely target its old ERM central rate from 1992 at 2.95 marks.
While Soros did not believe sterling would make EMU's launch on January 1, 1999, he did not rule out the possibility that it may join at a later date.
"I really don't think the pound will be in in the first round, that would be too fast," he said.
The Hungarian-born financier who has made millions speculating on the currency markets, said the dollar, which has also appreciated sharply in recent months, was not a worry.
"I don't think the dollar had appreciated too fast," he said. However, he added that the higher dollar had benefitted European economies.
The dollar has risen to 40-month highs against the mark this week and on Wednesday climbed above 1.75 marks in Europe.
On EMU, Soros said the chances of a punctual start for the single currency had improved.
"I would say that I am now 80 percent sure that EMU will start on time," he said.

In May, Soros said he was 75 percent sure the single currency would stick to the timetable for launch on January 1, 1999. However, after the French elections and the German gold crisis, he had upgraded the possibility.
"This proposition (that EMU would start on time) was tested in elections in France and the controversy over Germany's gold reserves and it passed the test," he said.
Soros said he had changed his mind on former EMU outside runners not making the first wave to join the single currency in 1999.
"I now believe Spain, Italy and Portugal will be in EMU from the start. A couple of developments have made me change my mind," he said.
"Germany and France have fallen behind with the Maastricht criteria and Italy has performed better than expected."

If Italy were in, Spain and Portugal would automatically be included as they are closer to the criteria laid out in the Maastricht criteria that countries must meet to join the single currency, he said.
Just a few months ago, Soros was less than optimistic that the three countries would be in EMU from the start.
Asked to comment on the flotation of the Thai baht, a currency which his funds have reportedly speculated heavily on in recent weeks, he declined to comment for fear of angering the Thai government.
"I don't want to comment on the baht because we've been attacked by the Thai government and there have been some exaggerated rumours," he said.
The Bank of Thailand stunned markets on Wednesday by abruptly changing its currency system, saying it would allow the baht to float and that the currency's value would be determined by market forces.
